title: Electrical Engineering
summary: From Ohm's law to feedback control. Three thresholds reorganise the subject: impedance (AC circuits as complex algebra), feedback (a system that measures its own output), and state (logic that remembers).
sources: Horowitz & Hill: The Art of Electronics
Agarwal & Lang: Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits
Harris & Harris: Digital Design and Computer Architecture

nodes.label: Ohm's Law & Power
nodes.summary: V = IR relates voltage across a resistor to current through it; P = VI is the rate energy is dissipated.
nodes.outcome: Size a resistor for a given current and check its power rating.
nodes.check: An LED needs 20 mA with 2 V across it from a 5 V supply. What series resistor, and what power does it dissipate?

nodes.label: "Voltage flows through the circuit"
nodes.summary: Voltage is a difference between two points (across); current is what flows (through). Mixing them up wrecks nodal analysis.
nodes.outcome: State what is 'across' and what is 'through' for each element.
nodes.check: Is it correct to say '5 volts flows through the resistor'?
nodes.answer: No: 5 V is across the resistor; a current flows through it.

nodes.label: Kirchhoff's Laws & Nodal Analysis
nodes.summary: Current into a node equals current out (charge conservation); voltages around a loop sum to zero (energy conservation).
nodes.outcome: Solve a two-node circuit with nodal analysis.
nodes.check: Three wires meet at a node: 2 A in, 0.5 A in, and one unknown. What is the unknown current, and which way?

nodes.label: Voltage Dividers & Loading
nodes.summary: Two series resistors scale a voltage, until a load draws current and changes the ratio.
nodes.outcome: Compute a divider output with and without a load.
nodes.check: Two 10 kΩ resistors divide 10 V. A 10 kΩ load is connected across the bottom one. What is the output?
nodes.answer: 3.33 V: the bottom becomes 5 kΩ, so 10 × 5 / 15.

nodes.label: Thévenin & Norton Equivalents
nodes.summary: Any linear two-terminal network looks, from outside, like one source and one resistance.
nodes.outcome: Reduce a network to its Thévenin equivalent and predict the current into a load.
nodes.check: How do you measure a black box's Thévenin resistance with a meter?
nodes.answer: Measure open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current; R_th = V_oc / I_sc.

nodes.label: RC & RL Transients
nodes.summary: Capacitors and inductors store energy, so circuits respond with exponentials of time constant τ = RC or L/R.
nodes.outcome: Predict a capacitor's voltage at any time after a step.
nodes.check: A capacitor charges through a resistor with τ = 1 ms. What fraction of the final voltage has it reached at 1 ms, and when is it 'done'?
nodes.answer: About 63%; after about 5τ = 5 ms it is above 99%.

nodes.label: AC, Phasors & Impedance
nodes.summary: Sinusoids become complex numbers, capacitors and inductors become impedances 1/jωC and jωL, and AC circuits become Ohm's law again. Troublesome because 'imaginary' current is real.
nodes.outcome: Compute the impedance of a series RC at a given frequency.
nodes.check: What happens to a capacitor's impedance as frequency rises?
nodes.answer: It falls (|Z| = 1/ωC): capacitors pass high frequencies and block DC.

nodes.label: Filters & Frequency Response
nodes.summary: Circuits treat frequencies differently; the Bode plot shows gain and phase against frequency.
nodes.outcome: Design a first-order low-pass filter for a cutoff frequency.
nodes.check: What is the cutoff frequency of an RC low-pass with R = 1 kΩ, C = 1 µF?

nodes.label: Diodes & Rectification
nodes.summary: A one-way valve for current with a forward drop of ~0.6–0.7 V (silicon).
nodes.outcome: Analyse a half-wave rectifier with a smoothing capacitor.
nodes.check: Why is a diode placed across a relay coil driven by a transistor?
nodes.answer: To give the coil's stored energy a path when switched off, clamping the voltage spike that would destroy the transistor.

nodes.label: Transistors as Switches & Amplifiers
nodes.summary: A small control signal (base current or gate voltage) governs a large current: the basis of every switch and amplifier.
nodes.outcome: Use a MOSFET to switch a load from a microcontroller pin.
nodes.check: Why use a transistor rather than driving a 1 A motor straight from a microcontroller pin?
nodes.answer: A pin can source only ~20–40 mA; the transistor lets the pin's tiny signal switch the large current.

nodes.label: Op-Amps & Negative Feedback
nodes.summary: Huge open-loop gain tamed by feedback: the output does whatever makes the inputs equal. Feedback trades gain for precision.
nodes.outcome: Design an inverting amplifier with a given gain.
nodes.check: An inverting amplifier has R_in = 1 kΩ and R_f = 10 kΩ. What is its gain?

nodes.label: Boolean Logic & Gates
nodes.summary: AND, OR, NOT and their combinations, simplified with Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps.
nodes.check: Which two gates make a half-adder, and for which outputs?
nodes.answer: XOR gives the sum bit; AND gives the carry.

nodes.label: Flip-Flops & Sequential Logic
nodes.summary: Feedback in logic creates memory; a clock decides when state changes. Troublesome because output now depends on history.
nodes.outcome: Design a 2-bit counter from D flip-flops.
nodes.check: What does a D flip-flop do on a rising clock edge?
nodes.answer: It copies D to Q and holds that value until the next rising edge.

nodes.label: "Sampling a bit faster than the signal is enough"
nodes.summary: Sampling below twice the highest frequency folds it into a false, lower frequency (aliasing).
nodes.outcome: Predict the alias frequency of an undersampled sine.
nodes.check: A 900 Hz tone is sampled at 1000 Hz. What frequency appears?

nodes.label: Sampling, ADC & DAC
nodes.summary: Turning continuous voltages into numbers and back: resolution, reference voltage, and the Nyquist rate.
nodes.outcome: Choose sample rate and resolution for a sensor.
nodes.check: A 10-bit ADC with a 3.3 V reference reads 512. What voltage is that?

nodes.label: Signals, Systems & Laplace
nodes.summary: Linear time-invariant systems are fully described by their impulse response, or by a transfer function in s.
nodes.outcome: Derive the transfer function of an RC circuit.
nodes.check: What property lets you predict an LTI system's response to any input from its impulse response?
nodes.answer: Superposition plus time invariance: the output is the convolution of input and impulse response.

nodes.label: Feedback Control & PID
nodes.summary: Measure, compare with the setpoint, correct: proportional, integral and derivative action, and the stability trade-off.
nodes.outcome: Tune a PID loop and explain the effect of each term.
nodes.check: A P-only controller leaves a steady error. Which term removes it?
nodes.answer: The integral term, which keeps growing while any error remains.

nodes.label: "Ground is where current disappears"
nodes.summary: Ground is just the reference node; every current that leaves a source returns to it in a loop.
nodes.outcome: Trace the complete return path of a current.
nodes.check: Current flows from a battery through a lamp to 'ground'. Where does it go next?
nodes.answer: Back to the battery's negative terminal: ground is part of the loop, not a sink.
